source_fact_map.fact: The supplied Atlantic page is a catalog of incidents ranked subjectively for outlandishness and importance; the accessed text does not state a continuing guardrail effect.
source_fact_map.quote: What follows is a catalog of incidents, ranked—highly subjectively!—according to both their outlandishness and their importance.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: Our 2016 editorial was a repudiation of Donald Trump’s character as much as it was an endorsement of Hillary Clinton for president. It was not meant to be partisan. The Atlantic’s founders promised their readers that we would be “of no party or clique.” This remains a core governing principle of the magazine today. What follows is a catalog of incidents, ranked—highly subjectively!—according to both their outlandishness and their importance. In most any previous presidency, Democratic or Republican, each moment on this list would have been unthinkable.

source_fact_map.fact: The linked video describes the project as an analysis of 50 norm-bending, destructive, and improbable events, and attributes its nonpartisan characterization to Jeffrey Goldberg.
source_fact_map.quote: 50 of the most norm-bending, destructive, and improbable events of Trump’s presidency to date.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: That was an understatement, argues editor in chief Jeffrey Goldberg. In a new Atlantic Argument, Goldberg elucidates The Atlantic’s decision to analyze 50 of the most norm-bending, destructive, and improbable events of Trump’s presidency to date. “This is not a partisan exercise,” Goldberg says in the video. “Our list is comprised of incidents that we can’t imagine happening in any other presidency, Republican or Democratic.”
